newsitem.title: USA: Russia debt rescheduling on track -- US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Russia debt rescheduling on track -- US analysts.

text.p: Russia's plan to sign a debt restructuring agreement with the London Club of banks in June confirmed that the refinancing remains on schedule, U.S. analysts said.
Amid confusion over the timetable of the restructuring, Russia Vnesh loans rallied but failed to sustain the gains.
"I think people may be confused that June is an earlier date, which I don't think it is," said Eric Nielsen, vice president and a senior economist at Goldman Sachs.
Some investors may have mistakenly thought Russia expected to complete the rescheduling in June, rather than merely outlining the legal details, Nielsen said.

Russia said Wednesday that by June 30 it will iron out the wrinkles of an agreement made in principle with the London Club two years ago. The agreement sketched plans for repayment of $25.5 billion of principal over 25 years and $7 billion in past-due interest over 20 years.
Dollar-denomited Vnesh loans RUVNUSLNS=RR rallied in Europe after the announcement but gave back most gains by early afternoon in New York.
Russia must reconcile $20 billion of the outstanding amount in order to sign the deal, and it expects arrangements for interest payments to individual banks to be completed sometime in August.
The large number of institutions holding former Soviet Union debt and the complexity of the loan agreements make the recononciliation process difficult, analysts said.
Despite some possible confusion, the announcement is good news in its own right, some analysts said.
"Regardless of how substantive it is, (the announcement) gives deal risk an excuse to tighten in," said Dan Peirce, chief emerging markets strategist at Bank of Boston.
Once rescheduled, portions of the outstanding interest will be converted to more-liquid Past Due Interest (PDI) bonds, experts said.
"The past-due interest, to the extent it won't be paid in cash, will be paid via issuance of PDI bonds," said Kurt Schmid, head of proprietary trading at SBC Warburg.
Schmid said he was unsure whether late June seemed a realistic target.
"The best news, I think, is that definitely the package will become effective prior to year-end," he said.
When-issued trading in the Vnesh loans was set to expire in December, he explained.
